content:
TPIL4 is based on v4.26. What major changes from v4.27–v4.32 should learners be aware of? I know a little bit about grind (but even omega is not included in TPIL), from the release notes, there are new do, sym =>, LCNF, etc., but I'd appreciate a more complete summary. Or should I directly learn from the Lean Language Reference instead? Any recommended resources?

I'm new here, I don't know whether this is the correct place to ask this.

I think this depends on your interest in Lean. If you are interested in proving theorems about mathematical objects, grind is the only thing that comes to mind. If you are interested in (meta-)programming or program verification then there are probably more relevant changes, but this isn't something I'm familiar with.

In my view the current TPIL misses lots of relevant technical details, such as how does Lean judge two terms to be definitionally equal, opacities of defs, abbrevs, structures, classs, etc., and some needed knowledges about the elaborating process? Are there any other ways to learn these aside from the Reference?
The reference manual has more information about some of those topics (and is probably the better place for them): https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/

Definitional equality is a more complicated topic. There's a dusting of information in the reference, there's also this https://ammkrn.github.io/type_checking_in_lean4/type_checking/definitional_equality.html and for a more rigorous treatment this: https://github.com/digama0/lean-type-theory/releases/tag/v1.0 (you want main.pdf)

Thank you, Chris Bailey! For providing these materials. I'll look at them soon. All in all, my point is, would it be better if we introduce some of these in the beginner's tutorial, or at least mention the importance and provide some references of them?

I think that it's difficult to include when considering the range of experience of someone reading a beginner text. As with many technical areas (in general, not specific to Lean) there is perhaps a missing "intermediate" text where such topics might be a better fit.
